children: Goldman Sachs expects the S&P 500 (
) to deliver another strong earnings season as artificial intelligence investment drives an increasingly large share of corporate profit growth.
Consensus forecasts call for S&P 500 (

) earnings per share to rise 27% from a year earlier in the third quarter, according to an Oct. 2 report led by Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider. That would mark a slowdown from the 33% growth recorded in the second quarter after excluding accounting distortions. Goldman expects most companies to beat consensus estimates again.
AI winners dominate earnings growth

The headline growth rate masks an unusually concentrated earnings picture. Information technology and energy are expected to generate nearly 80% of the S&P 500's earnings growth for the quarter. Consumer discretionary and consumer staples are expected to post little or no aggregate EPS growth.

AI infrastructure companies alone are expected to account for more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth. The 10 biggest contributors are forecast to generate 68% of the index's growth, with Micron Technology
and Nvidia
together accounting for more than one-third. Micron has already reported, posting year-over-year earnings growth of 1,003% and beating consensus estimates.

The concentration extends to stock-market performance. The S&P 500 was only 2% below its record high when Goldman published the report, while the median constituent was 17% below its own record. Goldman said market breadth had fallen to its lowest level since the dot-com bubble, with information technology supporting much of the index's earnings and returns.
Typical company faces tougher quarter
For the median S&P 500 (

) company, the outlook is considerably less spectacular. Consensus forecasts call for EPS growth of 9%, down from 14% in the second quarter. Revenue growth for the median company is expected to slow to 6% from 7%.

Margins also could face pressure. Consensus forecasts put the median company's third-quarter net margin at 14.7%, compared with 15.1% in the previous quarter. Analysts have cut median margin estimates by 11 basis points since the quarter began as companies contend with higher input costs. Information technology was the only sector where margin estimates weren't reduced.

Goldman nevertheless sees reasons for earnings to outperform expectations. Recent economic growth has remained strong and earnings revision breadth has stayed positive. The firm estimates nominal U.S. GDP grew about 6% from a year earlier during the third quarter.
Investors will look for returns on AI spending

The coming reports could also provide another test of whether enormous AI investments are translating into revenue. Consensus forecasts call for hyperscaler capital spending to jump 116% from a year earlier in the third quarter, accelerating from 87% growth in the second quarter. Goldman expects hyperscaler capex to grow more than 50% in 2027 and exceed the roughly $1.1 trillion currently embedded in consensus forecasts.
Goldman's analysts expect combined cloud revenue growth at Amazon
, Alphabet
, Microsoft
and Oracle

to accelerate to 55% in the third quarter from 48% in the second. Continued evidence that AI spending is generating revenue will be important for both hyperscaler shares and expectations for future capital spending.

Companies have been less forthcoming about AI's impact on productivity. About half of S&P 500 companies discussed AI in connection with productivity or efficiency during their previous earnings calls, but only 2% quantified the impact on earnings. Goldman expects more companies to disclose measurable benefits over coming quarters.
Accounting boost should fade

One tailwind from earlier this year is unlikely to repeat. Mega-cap technology companies recorded about $150 billion in accounting profits from rising values of equity investments during the second quarter. Those gains represented roughly 12% of S&P 500 EPS. Goldman doesn't expect a comparable contribution in the third quarter because major private investments didn't appear to appreciate as sharply.

Tariff refunds could provide a smaller offset. Companies received about $69 billion in refunds during the third quarter after $77 billion in the second quarter. Each amount was equivalent to roughly 6% of U.S. corporate pretax profits, according to Goldman.
Goldman maintains bullish S&P 500 targets

Goldman's broader outlook remains constructive. The firm forecasts S&P 500 EPS of $375 for 2026, up 36% from 2025, followed by $415 in 2027. Its year-end 2026 S&P 500 target is 8,000, while its 12-month target is 8,700. Based on the index level used in the report, those targets implied returns of about 4% and 13%, respectively.

For investors, the third-quarter season may therefore be less about whether aggregate earnings remain strong than about how widely that strength spreads. Goldman expects another quarter of solid headline growth, but AI infrastructure spending remains responsible for an unusually large portion of the gains.
